props.title: 4 for Texas

sections.content: **4 for Texas** (1963) represents a unique entry in the Western-comedy genre, starring Frank Sinatra and Dean Martin at the height of their Rat Pack fame. Director Robert Aldrich, fresh off the success of **Whatever Happened to Baby Jane?** (1962), attempted to blend Western action with Rat Pack swagger, creating an unusual hybrid that influenced later comedy Westerns like **Blazing Saddles** (1974). The film's mix of gunslinging and wisecracks set against a Galveston backdrop showcases a different side of the Western genre than contemporaries like **The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance** (1962).

sections.content: The early 1960s marked a transitional period for Westerns, as traditional offerings gave way to more experimental takes on the genre. While **4 for Texas** (1963) played with comedy, films like **A Fistful of Dollars** (1964) revolutionized the genre's visual style and tone. The presence of Ursula Andress, fresh from her iconic role in **Dr. No** (1962), also signals Hollywood's changing attitudes toward sexuality and glamour in Westerns.

Director Robert Aldrich's approach to **4 for Texas** (1963) differs significantly from his later Western **Ulzana's Raid** (1972), showing his range within the genre. The film's lighter tone and emphasis on star power over traditional Western elements reflects the industry's attempts to modernize the genre for 1960s audiences, similar to **Cat Ballou** (1965) and **Support Your Local Sheriff!** (1969). sections.content: The Rat Pack's influence on Western comedy extends beyond **4 for Texas** (1963). Dean Martin would go on to star in the successful **The Sons of Katie Elder** (1965) and the Matt Helm spy series, while Sinatra's Western appearances remained limited. Their natural chemistry and comedic timing influenced later buddy Westerns like **Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid** (1969).
